questions.question: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, why can't you say '2 g of hydrogen reacts with 1 g of oxygen'?
questions.solution: Coefficients count PARTICLES (molecules/moles), not masses: 2 mol H₂ (4 g) react with 1 mol O₂ (32 g). Mass ratios follow from molar masses, not from the coefficients directly. Convert mass → moles first, apply the mole ratio, then convert back.

questions.question: Why do equal volumes of H₂ and O₂ at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules even though their masses differ hugely?
questions.solution: Equal volumes at the same T and P contain equal numbers of MOLECULES (Avogadro's law) because gas volume depends on the number of particles, not their mass — the space between molecules dwarfs molecular size. 1 L of H₂ and 1 L of O₂ each hold ~2.7×10²² molecules, but the O₂ sample weighs 16× more (heavier molecules).

questions.question: Theoretical yield of a reaction is 25.0 g but 21.0 g is obtained. Calculate the percentage yield and give two realistic reasons for the shortfall.
questions.solution: % yield = (21.0/25.0) × 100 = 84%. Reasons: (1) side reactions consuming reactants to form by-products; (2) mechanical losses during transfer, filtration or purification (product left on filter paper, in solution); (3) equilibrium not fully shifted to products. Real chemistry never hits 100% — the yield measures how close the process got.

questions.question: Why is molarity temperature-dependent while molality is not, and when does the difference matter?
questions.solution: Molarity = mol/Litre of SOLUTION — the volume expands on heating, so molarity drifts. Molality = mol/kg of SOLVENT — masses don't change with temperature. The difference matters in colligative-property calculations and any precision work across a temperature range; chemists use molality there.

questions.question: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃: 2 mol N₂ with 3 mol H₂. Which is limiting and why is it NOT the smaller quantity?
questions.solution: 3 mol H₂ needs 1 mol N₂ (ratio 3:1); 2 mol N₂ would need 6 mol H₂. H₂ runs out first — H₂ is limiting despite being the LARGER amount in moles. The limiting reagent is decided by the stoichiometric RATIO, never by which number is smaller.

questions.concept: Why we balance equations at all
questions.question: Why is a skeletal equation useless for calculation until it is balanced?
questions.solution: Atoms are conserved, so any valid equation must have equal atom counts on both sides. Only a balanced equation states the true MOLE RATIO in which reactants combine and products form; an unbalanced one gives the wrong ratio and hence wrong masses. Balancing is not cosmetic — it is the statement of conservation of mass in mole terms.

questions.concept: Why percentage yield is never exactly 100
questions.question: A carefully run reaction still gives 87% yield. Give at least three independent chemical and physical reasons why 100% is unattainable in practice.
questions.solution: (1) Reversible side reactions consume some reactant. (2) Product is lost in filtration, washing, crystallisation or evaporation. (3) Impurities, incomplete reaction at equilibrium, and handling losses in transfers. Percentage yield compares actual moles to the stoichiometric prediction and is a statement about process efficiency, not about the chemistry being wrong.

questions.concept: Why gas volumes follow the mole ratio
questions.question: At the same temperature and pressure, 1 litre of N₂ reacts with 3 litres of H₂ to give 2 litres of NH₃. Why do the volume ratios equal the mole ratios?
questions.solution: Avogadro's law: equal volumes of gases at the same T and p contain equal numbers of molecules. So volume is a direct proxy for moles, and the stoichiometric coefficients are simultaneously volume ratios. This is Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes — a convenient shortcut valid only for gases under identical conditions.
